_comment: EVERY NUMBER IN THIS FILE IS AN ESTIMATE until a --meter run proves it, and treating one as fact is listed under 'Common mistakes' in CLAUDE.md. This is the money path: a credit is the unit a customer is charged in, so a wrong number here is not a wrong render, it is a wrong invoice. Nothing in scripts/auth/ hardcodes any of it -- one metered run has to be able to correct all of it in one edit, which is only true if there is exactly one copy. It supersedes config/pricing.json's `fal/video-UNVERIFIED` guess ($0.20/second, $3.00 per 15s) with a published formula plus a ratio, which is better evidence and still not a measurement.
_creditUSD_comment: ESTIMATE. What one credit is worth in ESTIMATED PROVIDER COST, and therefore the only thing that converts dollars into the unit on the button. Ten cents is a round, explainable number rather than a derived one, and it is a scale factor and nothing else: it is NOT the price a credit is sold at, and no code in scripts/auth/ multiplies it by anything a customer pays. Change it and every credit figure below moves together, which is the point. RAISED FROM $0.03 ON 2026-08-21, at Paul's direction, and the reason was legibility rather than economics: at three cents a tape cost 51 or 152 credits, which are ugly numbers that read as arbitrary and made the free tier look stingier than it is. At ten cents the same tapes cost 16 and 46. MARGINS ARE UNCHANGED -- every plan's creditsPerPeriod was rescaled in the same edit, so each plan buys exactly the number of tapes it bought before. This is the honest way to make the numbers friendlier: scale the unit, do not discount the tape. Selling 720p at '100 credits' while it costs 152 credits' worth of provider time would have been a 52-credit loss on every render, invisible until an invoice arrived.
_referenceSeconds_comment: The duration every estimatedUSDPer15s below is quoted at, and not a default so much as the contract: 375 frames at 25fps, asserted by ~200 tests. `creditCost` scales linearly from here for any other duration.
_aspects_comment: What a shape multiplies the tape's cost by, PER SHAPE rather than one number for everything that is not 4:3 -- because the multiplier is a property of the shape's pixel count and not of it being unusual. A 1:1 tape would be 0.75x, not 4/3, so a single 'non-default' constant would be wrong the day somebody adds one. ARITHMETIC, not an estimate, and the derivation is the whole justification: a resolution label names the SHORT edge (animate/plan.mjs `resolutionRaster`, the same rule section 13 uses for the tape raster) and 4:3 is the squarest shape this product ships, so 16:9 and 9:16 are exactly 4/3 the pixels at the same tier -- 854x480 against 640x480, 1280x720 against 960x720. fal bills tokens as pixels * seconds, by the formula in `provider` above which reproduces a real invoice to seven figures, so 4/3 the pixels is 4/3 the cost. The two are equal to each other because a portrait tape is a landscape one turned ninety degrees. THIS TAKES THE NON-DEFAULT SHAPES FROM 21 CR TO 28 AT 480p AND 46 TO 61 AT 720p, at Paul's direction 2026-08-29; 61 AND NOT 62 -- the multiplier applies to the dollar figure with the ceiling taken once ($4.5646 * 4/3 / $0.10 = 60.86 -> 61), where multiplying the already-rounded 46 CR gives 62 and charges a credit for a rounding step; the alternative he declined was a flat price, which would have sold the MOST POPULAR shape a third below cost, since 9:16 is the phone format and this product delivers to phones. A test recomputes these from the rasters, so an edit that invents a number goes red. WHAT IS STILL UNMEASURED: fal has never been ORDERED a non-4:3 shape, and it picks its own delivered raster -- 752x560 for an ordered 640x480, 1112x834 for 960x720. If its upscale differs by SHAPE rather than by tier, these move. Meter one wide render and correct them here; `npm run ledger` names the gap.

provider._comment: ESTIMATE, and PROVENANCE rather than the engine: `creditCost` computes from the estimatedUSDPer15s figures below, not from these fields. They are here because the 720p figure was derived from fal's published video token formula -- tokens = height * width * seconds * 24 / 1024, billed at $0.014 per 1000 tokens -- and a number whose derivation is not written down becomes folklore in about a month. A test asserts that the 720p estimate still matches this formula, so an edit that breaks the link is caught rather than absorbed. The 480p and 1080p figures are NOT this formula: pixel count is not the whole rate, because fal's fast Seedance tier tops out at 720p and the tiers are priced differently.
provider.source: fal published token formula, no invoice yet, UNVERIFIED

480p._comment:
MEASURED 2026-08-25, and the number moved UP. Two metered jobs (20260824-122201-af8b0d, 20260824-130457-a2e9ac) ordered 640x480 and were DELIVERED 752x560 at 24fps. fal bills the raster it returns, so the invoice is computed on 752x560: 148050 tokens at $0.014/1000 = $2.0727. The old figure of $1.51 was the formula applied to the raster we ASK for, which is not a raster that has ever arrived -- it understated every 480p tape by 37%, in the unsafe direction, and at 16 CR this tier was sold BELOW COST from the day it was priced.

THE NON-OBVIOUS RISK, and it is unchanged: 480 is BELOW the tape raster vertically (the tape works at 736x588 per config/render.json), so this is the only option upscaled before the grain goes on, and the only one that actually loses detail. The delivered 752x560 softens that -- it is closer to the tape raster than 640x480 was -- but it is still short of it.

THE DELIVERED ASPECT IS NOT 4:3. 752x560 is 47:35 (1.3429), where 720p delivered an exact 1.3333. Nothing downstream depends on it -- the tape stage crops to 4:3 -- but it is recorded because a tier whose delivered aspect drifts is a tier whose crop is throwing away a different amount of picture than the other one.
480p._raster_comment: WHAT THE RENDERER ACTUALLY ASKS FOR. Identical to width/height here, because the price above was already derived at the 4:3 raster. See the 720p row, where they differ, for why the field exists at all.
480p.source: MEASURED: fal usage page, two jobs, 752x560 delivered against a 640x480 order

delivered._comment: WHAT FAL ACTUALLY SENT AND BILLED FOR. This, not `raster`, is what estimatedUSDPer15s is computed from. Two independent jobs, same answer.

720p._comment:
MEASURED 2026-08-25 by job 20260824-225641-f34b4f, the first render that ever ORDERED a resolution. It asked for 960x720 and was delivered 1112x834 at 24fps: 326042 tokens, $4.5646.

THIS RUN SETTLED THE QUESTION THAT DECIDED THE PRICE LIST. Both 480p jobs came back 752x560, and if a 720p order had come back 752x560 as well then 480p and 720p would have been THE SAME PRODUCT -- and charging separately for them would have been a claim on a public page that is not true. It did not: 1112x834 is 2.20x the pixels of 752x560. The tier is real and can be sold honestly.

THE OLD FIGURE WAS RIGHT BY ACCIDENT. $4.54 was the formula applied to 1280x720 -- the 16:9 frame this product never orders and fal has never sent -- and it landed within three cents of the truth because two errors cancelled. A coincidence is not a derivation, so the anchor is now the delivered raster and the test asserts that link.

DELIVERED ASPECT IS EXACTLY 4:3 (1112/834 = 1.3333), which 480p is not. The upscale is 1.1583 on both axes, where 480p was 1.1750 x 1.1667 -- so fal upscales consistently but not identically, and neither factor is documented anywhere. It is measured, twice, and that is all.
720p._raster_comment: WHAT THE RENDERER ACTUALLY ASKS FOR, and it is NOT width/height above. THIS PRODUCT ALWAYS REQUESTS 4:3 -- the tape raster is 720x576 at SAR 16/15, i.e. DAR 4:3 -- so `720p` means 960x720 on the wire and nothing ever renders 1280x720. The two fields disagree on purpose and each is honest about a different thing: `raster` is the picture, `width`/`height` are the shape the PRICE above was derived at, and the open question in the _comment is exactly whether fal bills the raster it renders or the nominal frame. The higher figure is kept until a --meter run settles it. scripts/animate/plan.mjs derives the raster from the label (the number is the height, 4:3 gives the width) and scripts/providers/fal.mjs derives the same two rasters for its own resolution enum; a test asserts all three agree, so this row cannot drift away from what is requested without something going red.
720p.source: MEASURED: job 20260824-225641-f34b4f, 1112x834 delivered against a 960x720 order

delivered._comment: WHAT FAL ACTUALLY SENT. 24fps against a 25fps contract, which is where the once-a-second judder in every tape comes from -- 361 source frames stretched to 375 duplicates 15 of them, one every 25 frames.

1080p._comment:
DEFERRED, NOT CANCELLED, and its number is now an ESTIMATE BUILT ON A MEASUREMENT rather than on a ratio. Applying the 1.1583 upscale measured at 720p to a 1440x1080 order gives 1668x1251 and $10.27 -- 2.25x the cost of 720p. NOBODY HAS EVER ORDERED 1080p, so both the delivered raster and the price are forecasts.

WHY IT WAS DEFERRED, kept with the entry so that turning it on later is a one-field change rather than an archaeology exercise: roughly 2.25x the cost of 720p for pixels that are thrown away before the grain is applied, because THE TAPE RASTER IS 736x588 and 720p already covers it. Measured SSIM between a 720p-sourced and a 1080p-sourced delivery was 0.958 and the two were indistinguishable at 4x zoom.

THAT REASONING IS NOW SUSPECT AND SHOULD BE RE-TESTED BEFORE 1080p IS SOLD OR DISMISSED. The SSIM comparison was made against a 720p SOURCE back when nothing in this repo could actually order 720p -- every render silently took the provider default, which is why section 24 of CLAUDE.md exists. On 2026-08-25 an ORDERED 720p turned out to deliver 1112x834, a genuine step up from 480p rather than the same file, which is exactly the shape of finding the old comparison could not have made. One metered 1080p run settles it.

fal's own schema for this endpoint offers 480p, 720p, 1080p and 4k. Nothing here has read the 1080p page, and 4k is not in this file at all. Set `available: true` when there is a reason; `creditCost` refuses it until then rather than quietly rendering something else.
1080p._raster_comment: Recorded for the same reason the rest of this row is: turning 1080p on later should be a field, not an archaeology exercise. Nothing may request it while `available` is false -- creditCost throws, and so does resolutionRaster in scripts/animate/plan.mjs.
1080p.source: ESTIMATE: the 1.1583 upscale measured at 720p applied to a 1440x1080 order, UNVERIFIED

delivered._comment: A FORECAST, NOT A MEASUREMENT -- the 1.1583 upscale measured at 720p, applied to a 1440x1080 order. No 1080p job has ever run. `measuredOn` is null on purpose: a date here would make a guess look like an observation.

standard._comment: Not an estimate: a multiplier of exactly 1 is the identity, and it is listed rather than special-cased so the tier seam is exercised end to end before a second tier exists. A faster or higher-quality tier is one entry here plus one MEASURED multiplier. Do NOT add a speculative second tier -- an invented multiplier in the money path is a guess that bills somebody.

defaults._comment: What the estimate on the Record button is computed with when nothing else is asked for. 480p is the default because it is the cheap tier and the product is credit-conscious; 720p is the one that is worth paying for, and the page should say so.

packs._comment:
WHAT IS SOLD. A one-off bundle of credits, bought through Stripe Checkout, granted by a signature-verified webhook and by nothing else. Specified in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-24-credit-packs-pricing-design.md, which SUPERSEDED the subscription model on 2026-08-24 for two measured reasons: a tape costs $2.08 rather than $1.51 (fal bills tokens, and bills the raster it RETURNS), and the usage pattern is bursty -- three tapes in one evening and nothing for six months -- which a monthly subscription bills badly and cannot measure. A pack also answers the one question a subscription cannot: renewal is inertia, repurchase is a choice.

THE PRICE A CUSTOMER PAYS IS THE STRIPE PRICE, NOT priceUSD. `priceUSD` below is what this repo believes the Price says, and it is what the page prints and what the margin assertion in test/billing-packs.test.js checks. Stripe charges what the Price object says and nothing else -- there is no amount, no currency and no price_data anywhere in the checkout request, deliberately, so nothing a browser sends can change what is charged. If the two ever disagree, the Price is right and this file is stale.

NOTHING CAN BE BOUGHT WHILE stripePriceId IS null. A Price is immutable in Stripe, so creating one is the LAST step and it is gated on section 7 of the spec: meter the parked 720p job, fix the estimator so --dry-run can tell 480p from 720p, and run the blind check. Until then POST /api/billing/checkout answers 503 and the button on /pricing is disabled with a sentence saying why.

starter._comment:
THE ENTRY RUNG. $12 for 92 credits, decided by Paul on 2026-08-27, and it SUPERSEDES the $10/40 CR pack this key used to hold.

92 IS NOT A ROUND NUMBER AND IT IS NOT MEANT TO BE. It is 2 x 46, the smallest pool that funds TWO 720p tapes, and the 720p count is what this rung is sold on. The 480p count falls out of the same pool at four, and that is not a choice either: a 720p tape costs 2.19x a 480p one, so anything that affords two 720p tapes affords four 480p tapes. Paul asked for three-and-two. THREE-AND-TWO DOES NOT EXIST -- 3 x 480p needs 63..83 CR and 2 x 720p needs 92..137 CR, and those ranges do not overlap. Four-and-two was chosen over three-and-one because the 720p number is the one that separates this rung from the free grant.

MARGIN IS DELIBERATELY THIN AND THIS IS THE RECORD OF THAT DECISION. $12 for 92 CR is $0.130 a credit against a $0.10 cost basis: $9.20 of provider spend on a $12 sale, 23.3% gross and 17.9% after Stripe's 2.9% + 30c. The credit-packs spec (section 2.3) priced credits at $0.25 for a 2.5x cost basis, and this is HALF that. It is an acquisition price, taken knowingly, not a arithmetic slip.

WHAT THE THIN MARGIN COSTS, and it is a real thing that has to be decided rather than discovered: section 2.3 chose $0.25 partly so the margin 'absorbs one regenerate in six', because direct mode deleted the cheap rejection gate and a bad likeness now costs a whole tape. AT $0.130 A CREDIT THERE IS NO SUCH HEADROOM. One free regenerate on this rung is roughly a break-even sale. A free-regenerate policy is now a decision with a price on it, and it is NOT funded by this number.
starter.label: Starter
starter.source: Paul, 2026-08-27. Credits derived from the MEASURED 46 CR cost of a 720p tape. LIVE Stripe Price created 2026-08-31 on Timestamp's own live account (acct_1UAGgQPFjb61BCp6) -- this one charges real cards. The test Price it replaced lived on a sandbox belonging to another product and could not be promoted: a Price is immutable and lives in one mode on one account, so going live meant creating it again. Tax is EXCLUSIVE -- Stripe adds VAT on top and remits it, so a German buyer pays $14.28 on this rung; /pricing says so.

standard._comment:
THE SECOND RUNG. $19 for 138 credits, decided by Paul on 2026-08-27, and $19 rather than $25 for a stated reason: a $7 gap is a step somebody takes without deliberating and a $13 gap is one they think about.

138 IS 3 x 46 EXACTLY, the smallest pool that funds THREE 720p tapes, and it funds six 480p tapes at the same time. Unlike the entry rung, the number Paul asked for here IS achievable -- six-and-three is what 138 credits buys, precisely.

THIS RUNG'S RATE IS WORSE THAN THE ONE BELOW IT, ON PURPOSE. $0.1377 a credit against starter's $0.1304 -- 6% worse -- which is the INVERSE of the volume discount a credit ladder normally has. It is deliberate and it runs in this product's favour: 27.4% gross here against 23.3% below, so the rung a customer upgrades to is the rung that earns more. It is invisible on /pricing, which prints tape counts and never a per-credit rate, and the value story a reader actually sees is honest -- $7 more buys two more 480p tapes and one more 720p tape.

DO NOT 'FIX' THIS BY ADDING CREDITS. Raising 138 toward a proper volume discount lowers the margin on the rung that is currently carrying the ladder: at $19, every credit added here costs 10c of provider spend straight off the top. The old `archive` plan died of exactly this -- it drifted to $0.188 a credit against a $10 pack at $0.250, a bigger commitment at a better rate and a 47% margin, and nothing went red when it happened.
standard.label: Standard
standard.source: Paul, 2026-08-27. Credits derived from the MEASURED 46 CR cost of a 720p tape. LIVE Stripe Price created 2026-08-31 on Timestamp's own live account (acct_1UAGgQPFjb61BCp6) -- this one charges real cards. Tax is EXCLUSIVE, as on the rung above.

grant._comment: ESTIMATE in the sense that the cadence is a product decision nobody has taken yet. NOTHING GRANTS ON A PERIOD TODAY: periodDays is read by no code anywhere (verified by grep across scripts/ and test/ on 2026-08-29), and the only grant that exists is the one-time signup grant inside createAccount. The key stays because the cadence decision is still open, but copy written from this file must not infer recurrence from it -- the signup page said 'a free credit allowance every month' for exactly that reason, and the sentence was false. expiryDays is null, which means CREDITS DO NOT EXPIRE and the balance simply accumulates; if Paul decides they should not roll over, set it and realise the expiry as an explicit negative ledger entry, never as a silent adjustment -- credits vanishing without a ledger line is precisely the unauditable thing the ledger exists to prevent. DECISION NEEDED.

freeTape._comment:
THE ONE NUMBER THAT BOUNDS WHAT THIS PRODUCT CAN GIVE AWAY. Section 3 of docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-24-credit-packs-pricing-design.md calls the global ceiling "the single most important line in this section" and warns it is "the one most likely to be dismissed as paranoia". It is not paranoia, it is the only bound that exists: a free signup grants plans.free.creditsPerPeriod credits -- 21 today, one 480p tape -- which is $2.07 of MEASURED provider spend, against no revenue and no card on file. Nothing else in this codebase limits how many times that can happen. There is no rate limit on signup, no email verification (this build cannot send mail), and no payment on file to charge back against. Before this key existed, the exposure was $4.15 per signup -- the grant was 42 then -- multiplied by however many people found the page, and the difference between a good day and a drained fal balance was a number nobody had set.

globalCeiling IS A COUNT OF FREE TAPES ACROSS EVERY ACCOUNT THAT HAS EVER EXISTED, not per day, not per month, and not per account. It never resets. Reaching it is not an error state to be recovered from -- it is the product having given away what it decided to give away, and the correct response is a human deciding whether to raise it, not a cron job clearing it.

100 IS A PLACEHOLDER FLOOR CHOSEN TO BE SURVIVABLE, NOT A BUDGET DERIVED FROM ONE. At today's 21-credit grant it is 100 x $2.07 = about $207 of provider spend, total, forever, if every free account uses everything it was given. That is a number Paul can lose without the project stopping, which is the property a default in this position needs; it is emphatically NOT a claim that $415 is the right marketing spend. PAUL SETS THIS. Raising it is one edit and it is meant to be -- the whole design is that changing it requires reading no JavaScript.

CHANGING plans.free.creditsPerPeriod CHANGES WHAT THIS CEILING COSTS, and the two numbers do not move together on their own. This is a count of tapes, not a budget of dollars, because section 3 asks for "a hard maximum on free tapes across all accounts" and a count is the thing that sentence names. The consequence is real and it is written down here so nobody meets it by surprise: the grant WAS halved to 21 CR on 2026-08-25 -- section 3's own number -- and this ceiling's cost fell from about $415 to about $207 without this number changing at all. That is the coupling: doubling the grant would double it back the same way. If these two are ever edited apart, the exposure moves and nothing goes red.

ZERO IS THE KILL SWITCH and it is a supported value, not a degenerate one. Setting globalCeiling to 0 withholds the free grant from every future signup, immediately, while leaving signup itself working -- an account can still be created, still log in, and still buy a pack. There is a test for zero specifically, because a bound written as `granted > ceiling` rather than `granted >= ceiling` is correct for every number except that one, and zero is the value somebody sets at 2am while watching a balance drain.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO. It does not bound PAID spend -- a customer who buys credits may spend them, that is the product. It does not stop a single account rendering repeatedly, because an account can only spend what it was granted. And it is checked when the credits are GRANTED rather than, as section 3's wording suggests, before the render: the two bound the same dollars, because credits can only be spent once, and grant-time is the only one of the two that never shows a person a balance it will refuse to honour. That failure -- a visible balance the button rejects -- is exactly what CLAUDE.md section 26 finding 4 records as the reason the free plan had to move off 16 credits in the first place.

plans._comment:
WHAT A PLAN IS NOW, AND IT IS NOT A PRODUCT. Three entries live here and exactly one is offered -- the free signup grant. THE 'shelf' AND 'archive' TIERS WERE WITHDRAWN ON 2026-08-27, NOT DELETED (this comment said 'deleted' until 2026-08-29, while both rows sat forty lines below it; their own comments explain why they are deliberately kept -- they are the only paid-plan shape the accounts code branches on). Both were marked STALE AND NOT SOLD, both were sized against a 16-credit tape that has cost 21 since 2026-08-25, and both rendered on /pricing with no way to buy them. They also both printed "1 tape at 720p", because 48 and 64 credits floor to the same number against a 46-credit tape -- two dollars apart and identical on the page, which is the defect that prompted this rewrite.

WHAT IS SOLD LIVES IN 'packs' ABOVE. A plan is a grant; a pack is a purchase. Keeping the two concepts in one file is fine; keeping two competing PRICE LISTS on one page was not -- /pricing showed $10 twice, meaning different things each time.

DO NOT ADD A PAID PLAN HERE without turning subscriptions back on for real. Nothing in scripts/billing/ can charge a recurring price -- createCheckoutSession hardcodes mode=payment -- so a paid row in this block is a price with no way to pay it, which is exactly what shelf and archive were.

free._comment:
MEASURED-DERIVED 2026-08-25, and it has moved twice in one day. It was 16 credits, chosen when a 480p tape cost 16; the metered delivery put a 480p tape at 21 CR, so 16 bought NOTHING -- an account could sign up, see a balance, and be refused at the button. It went to 42 (two tapes) that morning, and to 21 (ONE tape) that evening at Paul's direction, which is what section 3 of the credit-packs spec specified all along.

WHAT IT COSTS US: one tape at $2.0727 is $2.07 of provider spend per signup, against no revenue and no card on file. Halving the grant halved that exposure without touching freeTape.globalCeiling, which is exactly the coupling the ceiling's own comment warns about: these two numbers do not move together on their own. THE GLOBAL CEILING NOW EXISTS -- see freeTape below -- so this figure is no longer multiplied by however many people find the page.

WHAT ONE TAPE MEANS, and it is the real cost of this choice: a person who gets one bad result has no second try before being asked to pay, and likeness is the thing being sold. That is the trade section 3 made deliberately. IT IS NOT ENOUGH FOR A 720p TAPE, and that is the shape of the free tier rather than an oversight: the free tape proves the likeness, and the paid tiers are what a person buys once they believe it. Zero is the only price in this file that cannot drift.
free.label: Free
